opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's one of the clearest natural experiments we have on the question of whether a society can simply opt out of a technological trajectory. Tokugawa Japan is often cited as the counterexample to technological determinism. In the late 16th century Japan was actually one of the most prolific adopters of firearms in the world. Portuguese arquebuses arrived around 1543, and within a few decades Japanese smiths were producing them in enormous numbers, and they were decisive in the battles that unified the country. Then, under the Tokugawa shogunate, the regime largely restricted gun production, centralized it, and froze military technology. Combined with the sakoku policy of limited foreign contact, Japan had roughly two and a half centuries of relative peace and technological stasis in the military domain. People like Noel Perrin wrote about this as "giving up the gun," and it gets held up as proof that societies can collectively choose not to pursue a powerful technology.

What I find powerful is that the story doesn't end there. It ends in 1853 with Commodore Perry's black ships arriving in Edo Bay. The Americans showed up with steam-powered warships and modern artillery, and the Japanese leadership could see immediately that they had no answer to it. They were forced into unequal treaties, and they had just watched what happened to China in the Opium Wars. Within about fifteen years the Tokugawa regime had collapsed, and the Meiji leadership embarked on one of the most rapid, deliberate programs of industrialization and military modernization in history, explicitly under the slogan of "rich country, strong army." Within a few decades Japan defeated China and then Russia.

So the lesson I draw is that a society can make a local choice to forgo a technology, but that choice is only stable as long as it's insulated from competition. Japan's isolation, as an island nation that could control its contact with the outside world, made the opt-out possible for a while. But once a more technologically capable power arrived, the pressures of military and economic competition essentially overrode that preference. The choice wasn't really eliminated, but the cost of maintaining it became existential.

That's what I mean by the limits of technological choice. I don't think technology is fully deterministic. Individuals, firms, and governments make real choices about what to build and how to deploy it, and those choices matter a lot, especially for the timing and character of a technology. But at the level of the broad trajectory, particularly for technologies that confer large military or economic advantages, competition between groups tends to select for adoption. Any group that declines risks being outcompeted, conquered, or forced to adopt later on worse terms.

And this matters enormously for how we think about AI governance. If you believe one country or one lab can simply decide not to build powerful AI, the Tokugawa case should give you pause. Unilateral restraint tends not to be durable. If we want to steer away from dangerous capabilities, or slow down in particular areas, it probably requires coordination that changes the competitive landscape itself, things like international agreements, verification, and shared norms, rather than relying on any single actor to step off the treadmill. The more hopeful corollary is that we have more leverage over which variants of a technology get built and how safely they're deployed than over whether the broad capability arrives at all. So I'd focus a lot of energy there: shaping the path, rather than assuming we can just refuse the destination.

r001.rationale: The response says Japan adopted firearms extensively, then the Tokugawa regime restricted and centralized gun production and describes this as “giving up the gun.”

r002.rationale: It says the choice was stable only while Japan was insulated from competition, then describes U.S. warships forcing unequal treaties and Japan’s subsequent modernization.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the Japan case is one of my favorite illustrations because it's almost a natural experiment in whether a society can opt out of a technology.

So for about two and a half centuries under the Tokugawa shogunate, Japan was remarkably successful at controlling its technological trajectory. It restricted foreign contact, it kept firearms marginal even though it had been a major producer of them in the late 1500s, it limited shipbuilding, it suppressed Christianity, and it maintained a fairly stable feudal order. And this wasn't accidental or because they were incapable. It was a deliberate political choice. The elite recognized that certain technologies and certain kinds of openness would destabilize the existing power structure, and they chose stability. And for a long time it worked. That's the important part. It's a genuine example of a society making a collective decision about which technologies to adopt and sustaining that decision for generations.

But then in 1853 Commodore Perry shows up in Edo Bay with steam-powered warships, and the whole edifice is revealed to be contingent on something Japan didn't control, which is what the rest of the world had been doing in the meantime. The Western powers had gone through the industrial revolution, developed modern navies, and were now in a position to impose terms. The Japanese could see very clearly what had just happened to China in the Opium Wars. And so the choice they faced wasn't really "do we want these technologies or not." It was "do we adopt them on our own terms, or do we have them imposed on us by others."

And what's striking is how fast and how thorough the response was. The Meiji Restoration essentially tears down the social order that the Tokugawa regime had spent centuries protecting. You get the abolition of the samurai class, you get conscription, railways, a modern navy, compulsory education, industrialization at a pace that was almost unprecedented. Within a few decades they defeat Russia in a war. So the society that had most successfully resisted a set of technologies becomes one of the most aggressive adopters, and the things they'd been trying to preserve are precisely what they ended up sacrificing.

The lesson I draw from this is that a society's freedom to choose its technological path is real, but it's bounded by the competitive environment. If you're isolated enough, or if everyone around you is making similar choices, you have a lot of latitude. But once a powerful technology exists somewhere in the system, the pressure to adopt it is enormous, because the alternative is being dominated by those who do. I sometimes frame this as technology having a kind of selection pressure on societies. The technologies that confer military or economic advantage tend to spread regardless of whether any particular society wants them, because the societies that reject them get outcompeted or coerced.

Now, I want to be careful not to make this too deterministic, because I think that's a mistake people make. Japan did have choices. It chose how to modernize, it preserved aspects of its culture, the emperor system, various institutions. And there are counterexamples where societies have successfully constrained technologies, like the nuclear nonproliferation regime or various arms control agreements, although those tend to work best when the leading powers coordinate. But the Japan case shows that the space of viable choices is narrower than it looks from the inside, and that it can narrow very suddenly.

And I think that's directly relevant to how we think about AI. People sometimes talk as if we could just collectively decide not to develop certain capabilities. And maybe in some cases we can. But the Japan case suggests that unless that decision is made at the level of the whole competitive system, or unless the leading actors coordinate, the pressure to adopt will tend to win out. So the question becomes less "should we build this" and more "what governance structures and coordination mechanisms could actually make a collective choice stick." That's the harder and I think more honest problem.

r001.rationale: It says Tokugawa Japan deliberately kept firearms marginal despite having produced them extensively, identifying a deliberate reversal of adoption.

r002.rationale: It describes Japan sustaining its path for generations until Perry’s arrival exposed its dependence on what Western powers had developed and forced the choice between adopting technology and having it imposed.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a striking example of the difference between a society choosing a technological path and being able to sustain that choice in a competitive world. Under the Tokugawa regime, Japan maintained substantial isolation and constrained its engagement with the outside world for a long time. So there was real scope for political choices to shape the society’s development.

But that autonomy depended on external conditions. When foreign powers arrived with superior military technology, Japan faced a much narrower set of options. Preserving the existing order became costly in a way it hadn’t been before. The subsequent Meiji transformation involved embracing industrialisation and building the military and institutional capacity to compete with those powers.

The lesson I draw isn’t that technology determines everything, or that societies have no choices. It’s that the choices available to one society depend on what other societies do. You might prefer to forgo a technology, but if it gives others a decisive advantage, maintaining that preference can mean sacrificing your ability to determine your own future. That’s an important constraint on how we think about governing powerful technologies.

r001.rationale: The response discusses Tokugawa Japan’s isolation and constrained foreign engagement, but does not mention firearms or a deliberate reversal of their adoption.

r002.rationale: It says Japan’s autonomy depended on external conditions and that foreign powers’ arrival narrowed its options, but does not clearly explain that Japan could sustain its path only while Western powers refrained from forcibly imposing change.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find striking is the contrast between how much control a society can exercise internally and how little control it may have over the broader environment in which it sits. Under the Tokugawa regime, Japan was able to restrict foreign contact and constrain certain kinds of technological and social change for a very long time. So it’s a useful corrective to the idea that technology simply develops autonomously and societies have to accept it.

But that autonomy had limits. If other societies develop technologies that give them substantially greater military power, they can eventually force the question. The arrival of foreign powers made maintaining the existing order much harder, and the Meiji response was to pursue rapid modernization.

So I wouldn’t take the lesson to be that societies have no technological choices. They clearly do. It’s that those choices are constrained by what other societies are doing. A country might prefer a particular way of life, but if sustaining it leaves that country unable to defend itself, it may have to adopt technologies—and accompanying institutional changes—that it would otherwise have rejected. That’s one reason international competition is so important to understanding technological change.

r001.rationale: The response says Tokugawa Japan restricted foreign contact and constrained change, but does not identify a deliberate abandonment or reversal of firearms adoption.

r002.rationale: It says Japan maintained its order for a long time and that foreign powers later made this harder, but does not clearly explain that this depended on Western powers refraining from forcibly imposing change.
